newsitem.title: USA: Tough US Senate fight seen for chemical arms pact.
newsitem.headline: Tough US Senate fight seen for chemical arms pact.

text.p: U.S. supporters of an international treaty outlawing chemical weapons called for support of the pact on Friday, saying its fate in Senate debate next week was in doubt.

"We're six days away from an enormously important vote in the Senate and no one has a clue whether this treaty will be ratified," Sen. Byron Dorgan, a North Dakota Democat, told reporters. He said the vote, scheduled for Thursday, was "very much in doubt."
Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota told reporters the treaty had a 50-50 chance of passing.

Dorgan appeared at a news conference with Democratic Sens. Tom Harkin of Iowa and Richard Durbin of Illinois in an effort to build support for the treaty one day after the Senate agreed to bring it to the floor for debate and a vote. A two-thirds majority is required for approval.

"Today we call on all of our colleagues to recognise that this treaty is in jeopardy, to speak up and to join in a bipartisan effort to do mankind a huge and historic favour and ratify this treaty," Dorgan said.

Under debate procedures agreed to on Thursday, the resolution of ratification, which signifies Senate approval of the treaty, contains five disputed provisions. Four of these would kill U.S. participation in the treaty if they are allowed to stand and its supporters will try to eliminate them, which requires only a simple majority.

The Clinton administration is mounting an all-out lobbying campaign for the pact, which goes into force on April 29, with or without U.S. participation. The treaty, already ratified by more than 70 countries, bars development, production, stockpiling, transfer and use of chemical weapons.
